description: Tear down a competitor's product by using it as a real customer for 30 days. Document every friction point, every delight, every missing feature. The teardown reveals their product decisions and where they are vulnerable.

steps.description: Select the competitor to tear down and sign up as a real customer using a real use case.

inputs.name: use-case
inputs.desc: A real use case you or a test user will execute with their product

outputs.name: signup-experience
outputs.desc: Detailed notes on the signup process: time to complete, friction points, first impressions, initial value delivered

outputs.name: teardown-plan
outputs.desc: The 30-day plan: which features to test each week, which use cases to run, what to measure

process: Sign up as a real customer, not a demo or trial (if possible). Use a real email, provide real information, and go through the same process any customer would.
Document the entire signup experience second by second: how long did it take, what information was required, how quickly did you reach value, what confused you, what delighted you.

Plan the 30-day teardown: Week 1 = core features and primary use case. Week 2 = secondary features and edge cases. Week 3 = integrations, customization, and support experience. Week 4 = billing, upgrade/downgrade, and cancellation.
Set up a structured note-taking system: for each session, record the task attempted, the steps taken, friction encountered, and your emotional reaction (frustrated, confused, delighted, neutral).

steps.description: Use the product daily for real tasks and log every interaction: what worked, what did not, what was missing, what surprised you.

inputs.name: use-case
inputs.desc: The real use case being executed

outputs.name: usage-log
outputs.desc: Daily log of interactions with the product: tasks attempted, time to complete, errors encountered, workarounds needed, features discovered, features missed

outputs.name: friction-inventory
outputs.desc: Running list of every friction point encountered during the 30 days

process: Use the product for at least 30 minutes per day on a real task. Not a tour of features, but actual work that produces actual output.
After each session, record: what you tried to do, how the product handled it, how long it took, where you got stuck, and what you wish the product did differently.
Note the features you discovered accidentally (undiscoverable features are a UX debt) and features you expected to exist but did not (feature gaps).
Track the cumulative friction: does the product get easier over time (good learning curve) or stay consistently frustrating (bad design)?

steps.description: Contact the competitor's support team with a real question and document the experience from first contact to resolution.

outputs.name: support-evaluation
outputs.desc: Full support interaction documented: response time, quality of response, number of touches to resolution, channel used, overall satisfaction

outputs.name: support-comparison-notes
outputs.desc: How this support experience compares to your own product's support (where are you better, where are they better)

process: Submit a real support request about a genuine issue you encountered during the teardown. Use whatever channel they offer (chat, email, phone).
Time every step: time to first response, time to resolution, number of back-and-forth messages, and whether the issue was actually resolved.
Evaluate the quality: did the support agent understand the problem? Was the solution correct? Did they follow up? Was the experience personal or robotic?
Compare honestly to your own support. If they are better in any dimension, note it. Competitive analysis that ignores the competitor's strengths is useless.

steps.description: Reverse-engineer the product decisions behind what you observed: why did they build it this way? What tradeoffs did they make?

outputs.name: product-decisions
outputs.desc: The inferred product decisions: what they prioritized (speed, features, simplicity, enterprise, SMB), what they deprioritized, and the tradeoffs they made

outputs.name: vulnerability-map
outputs.desc: Where the competitor is vulnerable: features they neglected, user segments they underserve, pain points they have not addressed

process: Group your observations by theme. If the product is fast but shallow, they prioritized speed over depth. If it has many features but poor UX, they prioritized feature breadth over usability.
Infer the target user: who is this product designed for? What use case is it optimized for? The answer reveals who they are NOT serving well.
Map the vulnerabilities: pain points they have not addressed, user segments they underserve, workflows they make awkward. These are your opportunities.
The goal is not to copy their strengths but to find their gaps. A teardown that produces 'they are good at everything' was not done rigorously.

steps.description: Synthesize the 30-day teardown into actionable insights for your own product strategy.

outputs.name: competitive-insights
outputs.desc: The 5 most important insights from the teardown, each tied to a specific opportunity for your product

outputs.name: action-items
outputs.desc: Specific product, marketing, or sales changes to make based on the teardown findings

process: Select the 5 most important insights. An insight is important if it reveals an opportunity that: your product can address, the competitor is unlikely to fix quickly, and customers care about.
For each insight, write one action item: a product feature to build, a marketing message to create, or a sales talking point to add.
Document the teardown in a format others can use: a one-page summary of the competitor's strengths, weaknesses, and your opportunities.
Schedule the next teardown (different competitor) in 6 months. The competitive landscape changes, and a single teardown has a shelf life.

description: Test an idea with the minimum viable test before building anything: a landing page, a fake door, a manual version, or a concierge service. The test answers 'will anyone pay for this?' before you spend months building.

steps.description: State the hypothesis you are testing as a specific, falsifiable prediction.

inputs.name: idea-description
inputs.desc: The product or feature idea to test

inputs.name: target-audience
inputs.desc: Who you believe will want this

outputs.name: hypothesis
outputs.desc: A specific prediction: 'X% of [target audience] will [take action Y] when presented with [offer Z]'

outputs.name: minimum-evidence
outputs.desc: The minimum evidence that would confirm or reject the hypothesis (e.g., 50 people see the offer, 5 sign up = hypothesis confirmed)

process: Write the hypothesis as: 'If I present [specific offer] to [specific audience], at least [X%] will [take a specific action].' The specific action must involve commitment (paying, signing up, providing contact info), not just interest (clicking, liking, saying 'cool').

Define the minimum evidence threshold. Below this, you cannot conclude either way. A typical threshold: at least 50 people exposed to the offer, with a 10% action rate as the minimum for confirmation.

The hypothesis must be falsifiable. 'People will like this' is not falsifiable because you cannot define 'like.' 'At least 5 of the next 50 visitors will enter their email for early access' is falsifiable.
If you cannot write a falsifiable hypothesis, the idea is not yet specific enough to test.

steps.description: Choose the minimum viable test format that can validate the hypothesis with the least effort.

outputs.name: test-format
outputs.desc: The test type: landing page (measures signup intent), fake door (measures click-through on a non-existent feature), concierge (deliver the value manually to a few customers), or pre-sale (take payment before building)

outputs.name: build-estimate
outputs.desc: Time to build the test: should be 1-3 days, not 1-3 weeks

process: Match the test format to the hypothesis. If testing demand: landing page with signup form. If testing willingness to pay: pre-sale page with payment. If testing whether the product can deliver value: concierge (do it manually for 5 customers).
The test must be buildable in 1-3 days. If it takes longer, you are building a product, not a test. Strip away everything that is not necessary to trigger the action you are measuring.
Avoid tests that measure interest instead of commitment. A survey asking 'Would you use this?' always gets inflated yeses. A landing page asking for an email gets the real number.
If the idea involves a service (not a product), the concierge test is best: deliver the service manually to 5-10 customers and see if they value it enough to pay.

steps.description: Build the test in 1-3 days, drive traffic to it, and collect data.

inputs.name: test-format
inputs.desc: The type of test to build

inputs.name: target-audience
inputs.desc: Who to show the test to

outputs.name: test-live-url
outputs.desc: The live test (landing page, signup form, or pre-sale page)

outputs.name: traffic-plan
outputs.desc: How to drive 50-200 people from the target audience to the test in 1-2 weeks

process: Build the test with one clear call to action. No feature tours, no long explanations. One headline, one paragraph, one action button.
Drive traffic from the actual target audience, not from friends or general internet traffic. If the target audience is small business owners, post in communities where small business owners are.
Set a time limit: the test runs for 1-2 weeks. After that, you have enough data to decide, or you do not have enough traffic (which is itself a signal about the idea's market).
Do not optimize the test page during the run. Changing the headline or the offer mid-test invalidates the data. Run it as built, collect data, then analyze.

steps.description: Analyze the test results against the hypothesis and make a clear build/kill/pivot decision.

outputs.name: test-results
outputs.desc: The numbers: total exposed, total who took action, action rate, and comparison to the hypothesis threshold

outputs.name: decision
outputs.desc: Build (hypothesis confirmed), Kill (hypothesis rejected), or Pivot (interesting signal but different from the hypothesis)

process: Calculate the action rate: number who took action divided by number exposed. Compare to the hypothesis threshold.
If above threshold: the hypothesis is confirmed. Proceed to building the product. The test has provided evidence that demand exists.

If below threshold: the hypothesis is rejected. Do not build the product. The most common mistake is building anyway because 'the test was not set up right' or 'we did not reach the right people.' If the test reached 50+ target audience members and none converted, the idea needs to change.

If the data shows an unexpected pattern (people signing up but for a different reason, or a different segment converting), consider a pivot: same audience, different offer, or same offer, different audience.

steps.description: Capture what you learned from the test, regardless of the outcome, and apply it to the next idea.

outputs.name: test-learnings
outputs.desc: What was confirmed, what was surprised, what was learned about the audience, and what would be done differently next time

outputs.name: next-test-direction
outputs.desc: If pivoting: the specific change to test next. If building: the features to prioritize based on what drove signups.

process: Record the key learnings: what the audience responded to, what they ignored, whether they converted, and any qualitative feedback received.
If the idea was killed, the learning is still valuable: you now know what this audience does NOT want, which narrows the search for what they do want.
If the idea was confirmed, look at the data for feature priorities: what did people mention in the signup form or in follow-up messages? These are the features to build first.
File the test results for future reference. Over time, a library of test results builds intuition about what works and what does not.

description: Run a Jobs-to-Be-Done interview: interview recent purchasers about the moment they decided to buy. The 'job' is the progress they were trying to make, not the features they wanted.

steps.description: Select 8-12 people who recently purchased (or recently switched from a competitor) and schedule 45-minute interviews.

inputs.name: recent-customers
inputs.desc: Customers who purchased in the past 30-90 days

outputs.name: interview-list
outputs.desc: 8-12 customers scheduled for interviews, selected to represent different segments and use cases

outputs.name: interview-guide
outputs.desc: The JTBD interview guide with the four forces questions

process: Select customers who purchased in the past 30-90 days. Recent enough to remember the decision clearly, not so recent that they have not used the product yet.
Include variety: different company sizes, different use cases, different industries. You want to see whether the 'job' is consistent across segments or varies.
Schedule 45 minutes per interview. JTBD interviews require time to probe the decision timeline deeply.
Prepare the interview guide focused on the timeline: what was the trigger, what did they try first, what pushed them to search, and what pulled them to your product.

steps.description: Walk the customer through the decision timeline: from the first thought of switching to the moment of purchase.

outputs.name: timeline-narratives
outputs.desc: For each customer: the full story from trigger event to purchase, with specific dates, actions, and emotions at each point

outputs.name: trigger-events
outputs.desc: The specific events that caused each customer to start looking for a solution

process: Start with: 'Take me back to when you first thought about [solving this problem / buying this product / switching from what you were using]. What was happening?' Get the specific moment, not a general timeframe.
Probe the trigger: 'What happened that made you start looking? Was there a specific event, a frustration, or a conversation?' The trigger reveals the 'job' the customer was trying to get done.
Walk forward through the timeline: 'After that moment, what did you do first? What did you try? What did you search for? Who did you talk to?' Map every step from trigger to purchase.
At each step, ask about emotions: 'How did you feel at that point? Were you frustrated? Excited? Anxious?' Emotions reveal the real motivation, which is often different from the stated reason.

steps.description: Extract the four forces acting on the customer during the decision: push (dissatisfaction with current), pull (attraction to new), anxiety (fear of switching), and habit (comfort with current).

outputs.name: four-forces-map
outputs.desc: For each customer: the specific push, pull, anxiety, and habit forces, with quotes

outputs.name: force-patterns
outputs.desc: The forces that appear across multiple customers (the universal job)

process: For each interview, identify the push: what was bad enough about the old solution that they could not tolerate it anymore? This is not a feature request; it is a life or work situation that became intolerable.

Identify the pull: what about your product specifically attracted them? Not features, but the progress they imagined making. 'I could see myself finally getting my reports done in minutes instead of hours.'

Identify the anxiety: what almost stopped them from switching? Common anxieties: 'What if it does not work?' 'What if I lose my data?' 'What if my team hates it?' These are barriers you must address in marketing and onboarding.
Identify the habit: what kept them using the old solution for as long as they did? 'I was used to it' or 'Everyone on my team knows how to use it.' Habits are the inertia your product must overcome.

steps.description: Synthesize the interviews into 1-3 job statements: the progress the customer was trying to make, stated in their language.

outputs.name: job-statements
outputs.desc: 1-3 job statements in the format: 'When [situation], I want to [progress], so I can [outcome]'

outputs.name: job-priorities
outputs.desc: Which job is most common, most urgent, and most underserved

process: Look across all interviews for the common push and pull. The job is the progress that most customers share, stated as: 'When [situation], I want to [progress], so I can [outcome].'
If there are multiple distinct jobs (different segments hire the product for different reasons), state each separately. Typically there are 1-3 core jobs.
Prioritize the jobs by: frequency (how many customers have this job), urgency (how strongly the push is felt), and underserved-ness (how poorly current solutions do the job).
The job statements are not feature requirements. They are the lens through which all feature decisions should be made: 'Does this feature help the customer make the progress they hired us for?'

steps.description: Apply the job statements to product, marketing, and sales strategy.

outputs.name: strategy-implications
outputs.desc: Specific changes to: product roadmap (features that do the job better), marketing (messages that speak to the job), onboarding (reduce the anxiety forces), and competitive positioning (address the habit forces)

outputs.name: anti-roadmap
outputs.desc: Features currently planned that do NOT serve the core job and should be deprioritized

process: Product: reorder the roadmap so features that serve the core job get priority. Features that do not serve any identified job move to the bottom or are cut.
Marketing: rewrite the primary messaging to describe the job, not the features. 'Get your reports done in minutes instead of hours' is a job. 'Advanced reporting with 50+ templates' is a feature.
Onboarding: address the anxiety forces directly in the onboarding flow. If customers feared data loss, show the backup feature on day 1. If they feared complexity, start with the simplest workflow.
Competitive positioning: address the habit forces that keep people with competitors. If the habit is 'my team knows how to use it,' offer migration support and team training.

description: Score features by expected impact using ICE (Impact, Confidence, Ease) but weighted by the number of users affected AND frequency of use. A small improvement used daily beats a large improvement used yearly.

steps.description: List all feature candidates from every source: customer requests, internal ideas, competitive gaps, and technical debt.

inputs.name: feature-sources
inputs.desc: All places feature ideas come from (support tickets, sales feedback, roadmap, competitor analysis, team ideas)

outputs.name: feature-list
outputs.desc: Every feature candidate in one list, deduplicated, with the source and a one-sentence description

outputs.name: feature-count
outputs.desc: Total number of candidates

process: Collect feature ideas from every source: support tickets (what customers ask for), sales team (what prospects need), competitor analysis (what competitors have), internal team (what engineers and designers see), and analytics (what the usage data suggests).
Deduplicate: the same feature requested by 5 customers and suggested by 2 engineers is one feature with 7 votes, not 7 features.
Write a one-sentence description for each feature. If you cannot describe it in one sentence, it is too vague to score.
Do not filter yet. The scoring method handles prioritization. Filtering before scoring introduces bias.

steps.description: Score each feature's impact by: number of users affected times frequency of use times severity of the problem it solves.

outputs.name: impact-scores
outputs.desc: Each feature scored on impact: users-affected (1-10) x frequency-of-use (1-10) x severity (1-10)

outputs.name: impact-rationale
outputs.desc: For each feature: why the score was assigned, with evidence

process: Score users-affected (1-10): 1 = a handful of users, 10 = nearly all users. Use actual data: what percentage of users encounter the situation this feature addresses?
Score frequency-of-use (1-10): 1 = once per year or less, 10 = multiple times per day. A feature used daily by 50% of users has more impact than a feature used yearly by 100%.
Score severity (1-10): 1 = minor annoyance, 10 = blocks the user from accomplishing their task. A feature that unblocks users scores higher than one that makes a working flow slightly better.

Multiply the three scores. The product is the impact score. A feature with users=7, frequency=8, severity=3 scores 168. A feature with users=3, frequency=2, severity=10 scores 60. The daily-use feature wins despite lower severity.

steps.description: Add the Confidence and Ease dimensions to get the full ICE score.

outputs.name: full-ice-scores
outputs.desc: Each feature with Impact (calculated above), Confidence (1-10: how sure are we about the impact estimate), and Ease (1-10: how easy is it to build)

outputs.name: ice-ranking
outputs.desc: All features ranked by Impact x Confidence x Ease

process: Score confidence (1-10): 10 = we have hard data (analytics, customer validation). 5 = we have qualitative evidence (customer interviews, support tickets). 1 = we are guessing. Low confidence scores pull down features that might be impactful but are unvalidated.

Score ease (1-10): 10 = trivial to build (a configuration change or a small UI tweak). 1 = requires months of engineering. Ease scores prevent high-impact features from being prioritized when they take so long that other features would produce more total impact in the same time.
Multiply Impact x Confidence x Ease. Rank all features by the result.
The top 5-10 features by ICE score are the strongest candidates for the next development cycle.

steps.description: Use the ICE ranking as input (not law) for the final prioritization decision, considering dependencies and strategic value.

outputs.name: prioritized-roadmap
outputs.desc: The next 1-3 months of features, ordered by priority, with the ICE score and strategic rationale for each

outputs.name: deprioritized-list
outputs.desc: Features explicitly deprioritized, with the reason (low ICE, not aligned with strategy, dependency blocked)

process: Start with the top ICE-ranked features. Check for dependencies: does feature A require feature B to be built first? If so, B moves up even if its ICE score is lower.

Check for strategic alignment: does this feature serve the core job-to-be-done? A high-ICE feature that serves a secondary audience may be deprioritized in favor of a slightly lower-ICE feature that strengthens the core product.

The ICE score is a tool, not a decree. It prevents emotional or political feature prioritization by providing a data-based starting point. The final decision may deviate, but the deviation must have a stated reason.
Communicate the prioritized roadmap and the deprioritized list to the team. Transparency about what is NOT being built is as important as what is.

description: Map every friction point in user onboarding: each field, click, decision, and wait. For each friction point, decide: remove it, defer it, or reduce it. The goal is time-to-value under 5 minutes.

steps.description: List every step a new user takes from first landing to first value moment.

inputs.name: product-or-service
inputs.desc: The product or service being onboarded

inputs.name: current-onboarding
inputs.desc: The current onboarding flow as designed

outputs.name: step-inventory
outputs.desc: Every step listed: page load, form field, decision point, wait time, confirmation step, tutorial screen, verification step

outputs.name: step-count
outputs.desc: Total number of steps from landing to first value

process: Walk through the onboarding as a brand-new user. Record every action required: clicking a button, filling a field, choosing an option, reading instructions, waiting for a loading screen, verifying an email, setting up a profile.
Count everything. A form with 5 fields is 5 steps, not 1. A tutorial with 7 screens is 7 steps. A loading spinner that takes 8 seconds is a step.
Record the time each step takes. Some steps are instantaneous (a click). Others take significant time (fill out a profile, verify email, wait for approval).
Calculate total time from landing to first value (the moment the user gets the core benefit for the first time). If this exceeds 5 minutes, you have too much friction.

steps.description: Classify each step by whether it is essential, deferrable, or removable.

outputs.name: classified-steps
outputs.desc: Each step classified as: essential (must happen before first value), deferrable (needed eventually but not before first value), or removable (does not need to happen at all)

outputs.name: removal-candidates
outputs.desc: Steps that can be removed entirely without affecting the user's ability to get value

process: For each step, ask: can the user get value without completing this step? If yes, the step is deferrable or removable.

Essential steps are rare. Creating an account might be essential. Verifying email is usually deferrable. Filling out a profile is almost always deferrable. Watching a tutorial is removable if the product is intuitive enough.

For form fields: do you need this information before the user gets value, or can you ask for it later? Most fields can be deferred. Name and email might be essential. Phone number, company size, and industry can be collected after first value.
The goal is to reduce the path to first value to the absolute minimum number of essential steps.

steps.description: For each deferrable or removable step, design the change: remove it, move it to after first value, or simplify it.

outputs.name: redesigned-flow
outputs.desc: The new onboarding flow with only essential steps before first value, deferred steps after first value, and removed steps gone

outputs.name: time-to-value-estimate
outputs.desc: Estimated time to first value in the new flow

process: Remove all removable steps entirely. Do not move them; delete them.
Defer all deferrable steps to after first value. The user completes them in the second session, not the first. Examples: profile completion, preferences, integrations, team invites.
For essential steps, reduce friction: auto-fill where possible, provide smart defaults, reduce the number of choices, remove validation that blocks progress.
Calculate the new time to first value. The target is under 5 minutes. Under 2 minutes is excellent.

steps.description: Design the first value moment to be as obvious and satisfying as possible, so the user immediately understands why they signed up.

outputs.name: first-value-design
outputs.desc: The specific experience the user has at the first value moment: what they see, what they accomplish, and why it feels satisfying

outputs.name: value-confirmation
outputs.desc: How the product confirms that value was delivered (a success message, a result displayed, a problem solved)

process: Define the first value moment precisely: what does the user accomplish that they could not accomplish before signing up? This must be a real result, not a tutorial completion.
Design the experience around this moment. When the user gets their first result, make it visible and celebratory (without being annoying). Show them what they just accomplished.
Remove anything between the last essential step and the first value moment. No tutorials, no walkthroughs, no 'getting started' screens. Go straight from setup to value.
Test with 5 new users (who have never seen the product) and time them from landing to first value moment. Observe where they get stuck and iterate.

steps.description: Set up measurement to track onboarding performance over time: completion rate, time to first value, and drop-off points.

outputs.name: onboarding-metrics
outputs.desc: The metrics to track: completion rate per step, time to first value (median), drop-off rate per step, and first-week retention by onboarding cohort

outputs.name: improvement-triggers
outputs.desc: Thresholds that trigger investigation: any step with more than 20% drop-off, time to first value above 5 minutes, first-week retention below target

process: Instrument every step in the onboarding flow: track how many users reach each step, how long they spend, and how many drop off.
Track the funnel: what percentage of signups reach first value? This is the most important onboarding metric. Everything else is diagnostic.
Set thresholds for investigation: any step where more than 20% of users drop off needs attention. Any step taking more than 60 seconds needs simplification.
Review monthly. Onboarding performance can degrade as the product changes (new features add complexity, new user segments have different expectations).

description: Separate signal from noise in user feedback: one loud complaint is noise, ten quiet similar complaints are signal. Categorize by theme, count frequency, weight by customer value, and prioritize the most frequent theme from the most valuable customers.

steps.description: Collect all user feedback from every channel into one place.

inputs.name: feedback-sources
inputs.desc: All channels where feedback arrives (support tickets, NPS surveys, app store reviews, social media, sales calls, user interviews)

inputs.name: time-period
inputs.desc: The period to analyze (last quarter recommended)

outputs.name: feedback-corpus
outputs.desc: All feedback items in one list with: source, date, customer, verbatim text, and customer tier (if applicable)

outputs.name: feedback-count
outputs.desc: Total number of feedback items collected

process: Collect feedback from every channel. Support tickets, NPS open-text responses, app store reviews, social media mentions, sales call notes, user interview transcripts, churn survey responses.
Include positive AND negative feedback. Positive feedback reveals what to protect. Negative feedback reveals what to fix.
Attach the customer tier (enterprise, mid-market, SMB, free) to each piece of feedback. Not all feedback is equally weighted.
Aim for at least 100 feedback items for meaningful patterns. Fewer than 50 produces unreliable themes.

steps.description: Categorize every piece of feedback into themes and count the frequency of each theme.

outputs.name: theme-frequencies
outputs.desc: Each theme with: count, percentage of total feedback, and 3-5 example quotes

outputs.name: emerging-themes
outputs.desc: Themes that appeared recently but were not present in previous periods (new problems or shifting expectations)

process: Read through the feedback and tag each item with one primary theme: pricing, performance, missing feature, usability, support, reliability, onboarding, documentation.
Count the frequency of each theme. The distribution is usually Pareto-shaped: 2-3 themes account for 60-80% of all feedback.
Pull 3-5 representative quotes for each top theme. These quotes are more useful in product discussions than abstract theme labels because they convey the emotion and specificity.
Look for emerging themes: topics that appeared in the recent quarter but were absent in the previous one. These are early signals of a new problem.

steps.description: Weight each theme by the value of the customers who raised it: feedback from high-value customers gets higher priority.

outputs.name: weighted-themes
outputs.desc: Each theme with a value-weighted score: frequency x average customer value of the reporters

outputs.name: priority-themes
outputs.desc: The top 3 themes by value-weighted score, which represent the highest-priority product work

process: For each theme, calculate the average customer value (revenue or tier) of the customers who raised it. A theme raised by 5 enterprise customers (high value) may be more important than a theme raised by 50 free users (low value).
Calculate the weighted score: theme frequency x average customer value. This gives enterprise feedback higher weight without ignoring volume.
If a theme is raised by both high-value and low-value customers, it is doubly important: it affects both retention and growth.
The top 3 weighted themes are the product team's priority. Addressing these has the highest expected impact on both retention and revenue.

steps.description: Verify the top themes by checking whether they correlate with churn, low NPS, or declining engagement.

outputs.name: verification-results
outputs.desc: For each top theme: correlation with churn (do customers who mention this theme churn at a higher rate?), NPS (do they score lower?), and engagement (do they use the product less?)

outputs.name: confirmed-priorities
outputs.desc: Themes that are both frequent AND correlated with negative outcomes (these are verified priorities, not just complaints)

process: For each top theme, check the churn rate of customers who raised it vs customers who did not. If customers who complain about 'poor performance' churn at 2x the rate, the performance theme is confirmed as a retention driver.
Check NPS scores: do customers who raised this theme score significantly lower on NPS?
Check engagement: do customers who raised this theme use the product less frequently or less deeply?

Themes that are frequent, value-weighted, AND correlated with negative outcomes are the highest-confidence priorities. Themes that are frequent but not correlated with outcomes may be annoyances, not retention risks.
